chapter: Miles Davis stories and what jazz means
title: First drink, an alcohol culture, and the Berk fire
summary: Gil recalls drinking moonshine as a boy in an Idaho mining town and the town burning down while residents sheltered in a mine.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: It was an alcohol they made during prohibition. It was pure white, looked like water and they called it white & mule. I don't know how strong it was, but that was the first drink I had.
You think you were ten years old when you had it? (LAUGHTER). Do you remember what it did to you?

Yes I do. It made me throw up. (LAUGHTER). A lot of kids were drinking it though. In this town I lived in, a little town in Idaho called Berk and the kids didn't, there were no other drugs of any kind except alcohol. So I grew up on alcohol in that respect and this little town I lived in named Berk it was in a valley between two mountains. The mountains came right down like that and the valley wasn't any more than like, well say one block wide
that's all it was. And the road and the railroad and the people who walked, everybody all went up that one street. (LAUGHTER).

So one day a fire started about down about three or four towns in a town called Mason and it started blowing up that valley and I came running to my mother and said, there's a fire down in Mason I think it's going to hit this town, we'd better get our stuff and get out of here.

So we packed up all my mother's sheet music and mandolin and stuff like that and got out of the rooming house that we lived in where my mother was working and it was like a rooming house beanery. She used to get up at three o'clock in the morning to start the breakfast.

Anyway the fire started coming up sure enough. It did come up and it hit Berk and we all went down in a mine. They took us down in this mine and people brought all their belongings down there and the town burned down over us. The next morning we came out and there was no town. People were poking around looking for things and there was nothing left at all. The whole thing burned up while we were underground.
But you had your mother's sheet music and mandolin?
Yes. That's what she gave me to take with me.

And somebody salvaged a barber's chair and I can just remember that you know. I was just a kid and I had so much fun down there with that, sitting in that barber chair pumping it up and down. (LAUGHTER).
While the town burns down. (LAUGHTER). You were the mining camp Nero huh? (LAUGHTER). That was your own kind of fiddling huh? Fiddling around.

Certainly was. It was an alcohol culture really there. Most all the people that weren't that hadn't lived in the States very long that were recently from Europe, came from Sweden and Ukrain and a few places like that. We lived in a town called Odessa as a matter of fact in Washington, in the State of Washington.
